 Attempts are being made in Congress to enshrine the Hindu celebration day Diwali as the 12th federal holiday in the U.S., and the only religious feast day to be officially recognized apart from Christmas Day. It is notoriously difficult to get new federal holidays approved. Attempts by Republicans to make Easter Monday a holiday failed in 2025, and chances that the Diwali bill will pass are also slim. Diwali, also known as the Festival of Lights, is one of the most significant holidays of the year for many groups in the South Asian community, including Hindus, Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists, and more. The five-day festival takes place between November 6-10 this year, with 2027's festival scheduled to begin on October 27. In a bill submitted to Congress on Monday night titled the Diwali Day Act, Democratic Congresswoman Grace Meng proposes enshrining Diwali as a federal holiday as a rebuttal to the rising tide of South Asian prejudice. "Diwali represents the triumph of good over evil and knowledge over ignorance," Meng said in a press release. "At a time when anti-Hindu and anti-South Asian hate is on the rise, recognizing Diwali as a federal holiday sends a powerful message that Hindus, as well as Sikhs, Jains, and Buddhists, are valued members of our society. "Here in Queens, I see firsthand how meaningful Diwali is to so many families and communities. My Diwali Day Act will help educate Americans about the importance of this day, and I will continue working to create a more inclusive nation that honors the rich cultural traditions of its people." The bill has been resubmitted to Congress by Meng for the second time, after it was initially shot down in 2023. It currently has 19 co-sponsors, including Representatives Ro Khanna, Rashida Tlaib, and Josh Gottheimer. Despite the submission, it is unlikely the bill will make it into law. The last time it was submitted, it was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability and failed to progress past the committee stage. Anti-Asian Hatred on the Rise Meng, the chairwoman of the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus (CAPAC), has long been an outspoken critic of anti-Asian violence and prejudice. Hindu and South-Asian communities across the U.S. have seen an alarming rise in targeted harassment and racial hatred in recent months. Earlier this month, a Diwali celebration in Seattle was disrupted by far-right activists brandishing signs bearing racial slurs. It was organized by a group called "White Replacement," and led by a former January 6 rioter. In October, a neo-Nazi plot to stage a mass shooting at a Hindu place of worship in Aurora, Illinois, was also narrowly foiled by authorities. "We are horrified that a white supremacist attempted to carry out a mass shooting targeting Indian Americans at a Hindu temple in Aurora, Illinois, where CAPAC Member Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi and his family worship," Meng said in a statement. "The self-proclaimed neo-Nazi allegedly fantasized about murdering Indian people, wrote a South Asian slur on a gas canister, and described Indian, Jewish, and African American people as "subhumans." "This plot exposes the very real danger white supremacist ideology poses to our communities and houses of worship, and it cannot be viewed in isolation," she added. "We are witnessing the normalization of hatred that has escalated into real-world threats and violence against Indian and South Asian communities." What About Easter? Getting a new federal holiday approved is a difficult task, even for events widely celebrated by the population. Juneteenth, the last holiday to be enshrined into law, was created under President Biden in 2021, with Martin Luther King Day becoming a holiday under Ronald Reagan in 1982. Before that, the last public holiday to be made official was Columbus Day, now known as Indigenous Peoples Day, which was created in 1968. In 2025, Republican lawmakers attempted to make Easter a public holiday with a bill titled the Easter Monday Act. "81% of Americans celebrate Easter. But our current holiday schedule makes it way too difficult for families to celebrate together," said Senator Eric Schmitt, who introduced the act. "Easter falls on the longest unbroken work stretch of the calendar. March and April are the only back-to-back months without a federal holiday." "This isn’t a radical idea," he added. "Our holidays and traditions are part of the story we tell about ourselves. This is not partisan. It's not a 'Republican' or 'Democrat' holiday. It's an American holiday, allowing a fuller celebration of the defining moment of the faith that shaped our nation and civilization. The Easter Monday Act was read twice in the Senate and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, where it was stalled without any hearings, debates or votes held. A version of the bill was also introduced in Congress by Representative Riley Moore, which was referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform and was stalled much like its Senate counterpart.
